Top News
 
 
 
 Skies at a standstill 
 
 
 
Getty Images
 
 
 Operations from airlines like Delta ( DAL ), Southwest ( LUV ) and United ( UAL ) are slowly returning to normal following a historic nationwide ground stop on Friday. After all was said and done, 12,462 flights were canceled that day, while thousands more were scrapped on Saturday and Sunday. It was only three years ago that another FAA ground stop stranded travelers across the country, shedding a fresh spotlight on a traffic control system that needs some serious attention.

 What happened? The FAA said its outdated air traffic system got overwhelmed when a massive flood of connection requests (1,000 attempts every 4 to 5 seconds) started glitching out radar feeds and plane communications. An investigation traced the data surge to a site in Texas and another in Arkansas, where the FAA's network contractor, L3Harris ( LHX ), had just deployed a new router from Hewlett Packard Enterprise ( HPE ). The system immediately stabilized after both locations were blocked and the broadcasting function was disabled on the routers, but officials are still determining whether a faulty installation, configuration error, or hardware defect triggered the surge, with HPE insisting its equipment did not fail.

"Based on all available evidence, we have no indication that this was a cyberattack or an outside nefarious actor," the FAA declared in a press release . "This type of work has been going on for years to transition from old copper wires that are being disconnected due to their obsolescence." The FAA also outlined that the disruption was not part of the FAA's broader modernization effort or related to AI-supported air traffic management tools like the SMART system.

 Going forward: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will submit an itemized request to Congress today to provide $50B in emergency funding to upgrade aging air traffic control infrastructure. He had previously argued for $30B, after being awarded $12.5B for air traffic control upgrades last year. While that cash was locked into specific hardware such as radios and radar, Duffy says he now needs a lot more money for things like airspace management software. The push comes after a series of recent outages, staffing shortages, and close calls in the sky have put serious pressure on the FAA to modernize.
